newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Kabul residents flee as fear descends on city.
newsitem.headline: Kabul residents flee as fear descends on city.

text.p: The number of people fleeing Kabul has soared as fear descends on the city -- fear of yet another battle for one of the world's most battle-scarred cities, and fear of its new Taleban rulers.

Refugee officials say that in the two weeks following the capture of the Afghan capital by the purist Islamic Taleban at the end of September, about 125 people a day turned up at the main official crossing point into Pakistan.

Now the figure is nearly 900 a day, and that is only the official count. There are countless other ways into Pakistan and many people never register their arrival, staying with relatives and friends already there, officials say.
About 90 percent of the official arrivals to what has become the world's biggest refugee population -- some 1.4 million in Iran and about 1.0 million in Pakistan -- are from Kabul, they say.
Many Kabulis were happy when the Taleban arrived with their strict Islamic code to replace a government run by former guerrillas who were synonomous with corruption and theft.
Educated people began to trickle out following the Taleban ban on women working or going to school.
But the exodus is growing because, many Kabulis say, life is becoming intolerable.
Shopkeepers are hurting because people have little money to spend.

On Sunday, for example, civil servants received their first pay in two months. The average monthly pay of a civil servant in the Afghan capital is 102,000 Afghanis, or $6. Senior staff members earn the equivalent of between $12 and $15 a month.
The Taleban blame the shortage of money on ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, who they say took the central bank's reserves with him when he retreated from Kabul.
People say one reason so many Kabulis are leaving is fear of more fighting in the streets as a northern alliance battles, so far unsuccessfully, to reach the city.
But they say fear of the Taleban is even greater.
They accuse the militia of arresting people on whims, especially if they are from Masood's Panjsher Valley stronghold.
They allege that Taleban fighters beat people on the streets for not dressing in the approved style and threaten women for talking to men, even if they are only buying things in a shop.
They also say the Taleban force people into mosques for the main prayers on Friday, the Islamic day of rest.
The Taleban deny these claims.
"All Taleban are educated and cultured. They are sweet like this chocolate," Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told Reuters, tossing a wrapped sweet into a reporter's lap. "Taste it."
Stories to the contrary, he said, were propaganda spread by Masood and his ally, Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, who have joined forces to try to sweep the Taleban from power.

Mutaqi said no Taleban fighters were authorised to arrest anyone -- that was the job of the police. But Taleban are everywhere on Kabul's streets. Policemen, apart from those directing traffic, are not.

Kabulis say the Taleban persecution began to take on an ethnic flavor about two weeks ago when the largely ethnic Pashtun Taleban began searching Pansheri houses for weapons in apparent fear of an uprising in the city as Masood and Dostum's forces moved towards it.
"A jeep load of Taleban came and searched the house of a Panjsheri neighbour. They found nothing but arrested him anyway," said one man who asked not to be identified.

"As they were putting him in the jeep, an old Pashtun man from across the road told them he had known the man for years and he wasn't connected to Masood. They clubbed the old man with the butt of a Kalashnikov and left him lying in the road."
The man said the Panjsheri neighbour had not been seen since.
Witnesses say all jail cells in Kabul are full and relatives have a hard time finding people who have been arrested.

"The Taleban were very helpful, but we went to every police station in Kabul and still couldn't find him," said one Kabuli after searching for someone believed arrested. "The problem is they don't know who picked him up or why or where they took him."
"They kept me for two days and two nights and gave me no food," said one Panjsheri. "They never interrogated me, just beat me for five minutes with a thick belt until I fell down," he said.
"I've no idea why they picked me up, except that I'm a Panjsheri. The only reason I was released was that a Taleban recognised me and got me out."

Other Panjsheris say they spend all day away from home, going back only after dark. "If there's a knock at the door at night, I can get away. I can't do that in daylight. Anyway, it won't be for long. I'm getting out of here as soon as I can find transport," said one.

The Taleban are also confiscating cars and demanding drivers produce papers to prove they own them. That's not a problem for many Kabulis, who say many cars were stolen during the years of lawlessness preceding the Taleban takeover.
But the Taleban's actions nonetheless have many Kabulis dreaming of freedom across the border.
"A group of them came into my neighbour's shop and asked where he got the money to buy all his goods," said the Pashtun owner of a shop in the city centre.
"As soon as they left, he closed his shop and disappeared. I haven't seen him since, but I bet he's in Pakistan. Probably so are the others," he said, gesturing to a line of closed shops.
"I'll be gone soon as well," he added. "When I go home, I'm in prison. When I come to the shop, I'm in prison. There's nothing to enjoy, not even music or a movie."
Both have been banned by the Taleban.
